items.title: The 5 Qualities of Site-Specific AI Chatbots
items.summary: NN/g proposes five design qualities every site-specific AI chatbot needs — handoff willingness, flexibility, proactivity, emotional responsiveness, and transparency — as an early-stage checklist for teams building trustworthy on-product assistants.
items.why: The Cuemath tutor experience leans on AI-assisted help, and these five knobs — especially handoff and transparency — are the concrete UX levers you'd argue about when spec'ing a K-12 math chatbot that a kid and a parent both have to trust.

items.title: Building accessibility into a canvas-based product
items.summary: Figma engineers David Winslow and Elynn Lee explain how they made a WebGL canvas usable with screen readers and keyboards by maintaining a hidden 'Mirror DOM' — an invisible HTML tree that shadows the canvas so assistive tech has something semantic to walk.
items.why: A primary-source account of how a design tool actually pays the accessibility bill on a non-DOM surface — directly relevant when CueDesign or the practice app builds custom canvas-y interactions (drawing, geometry, whiteboard) that would otherwise lock kids and screen-reader users out.

items.title: AI Skills for Design Engineers
items.summary: Emil Kowalski has packaged his animation and interaction philosophy — easing, duration, when NOT to animate, button press feel, popover origins — as installable 'skills' that coding agents like Claude Code and Cursor can load to nudge their UI output toward taste.
items.why: This is exactly the design × AI workflow lean you care about: not hype, but a respected practitioner turning tacit interaction craft into machine-readable instructions — a template for how a design lead could encode CueDesign's motion/interaction rules into the AI tools engineers already use.

items.title: How to keep design teams steady through constant change
items.summary: Interview with Jen Dunnam (ex-Patreon, ex-Shopify, now VP of Futures at Hinge) on leading design teams through the AI churn — defining what 'speed' actually means for your org, hiring for rigorous thinking over tool fluency, and protecting the space to push back on shiny demos.
items.why: Concrete design-leadership tactics from someone who has run large product design orgs — useful framing when you're deciding how the Cuemath design team spends its AI-experimentation budget without letting every impressive demo set the roadmap.

items.title: NYC World Cup Campaign
items.summary: Designer Arsh Raziuddin's typographic campaign for the 2026 FIFA World Cup in New York — Dunbar Tall headlines and a customised Excelsior Script pull the five boroughs together with the visual energy of vintage sports memorabilia, stamps and passport marks.
items.why: A clinic in editorial-tier typography solving a mass-market brief with real warmth — the kind of confident type-driven system worth studying when Cuemath's brand or campaign work needs identity that feels handmade and human rather than SaaS-flat.
